summary: This standards-track RFC defines a SIP Usage for RELOAD, providing the function of a SIP proxy or registrar in a fully distributed system, with lookup of Addresses of Record stored in the overlay. It also defines GRUUs mapping a registration to a specific node.

eli5.summary: Phone-call setup without a central server: the participants collectively remember who is where.

questions: what is the sip usage for reload
how does p2p sip registration work
what is a gruu in reload
how does reload replace a sip registrar
subtitle: How phone-style SIP calls can find each other through a peer-to-peer overlay instead of a central registrar.

tldr.problem: SIP normally needs a permanent proxy or registration server to learn where a user can be reached. A fully distributed telephony service has no such server.
tldr.mechanism: Peers store their Address of Record in the RELOAD overlay as a SIP-REGISTRATION entry, look it up with a Fetch, and then use an AppAttach message to open a direct connection that carries ordinary SIP.
tldr.outcome: The overlay does the registrar and rendezvous work, and media never travels through it. The RFC also defines how GRUUs and domain restrictions fit in.

today: RFC 7904 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2016. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the RELOAD base protocol in RFC 6940.

sections.title: SIP Without a Central Server
sections.content:
RFC 6940 defines RELOAD, a peer-to-peer signaling protocol for general use on the Internet. RFC 7904 defines a SIP Usage of RELOAD. It lets SIP user agents set up peer-to-peer SIP (or SIPS) sessions without a permanent proxy or registration server, for example in a fully distributed telephony service. The overlay itself performs the registration and rendezvous functions that such servers normally do.

The Usage has two basic functions. Registration stores a mapping from a user's Address of Record (AOR) to a Node-ID in the overlay, and lets others retrieve it. Rendezvous uses RELOAD message routing to set up a direct connection once the Node-ID is known. Every operation is a standard RELOAD method.

RELOAD's only job in a call is to set up the direct SIP connection. After the ICE checks finish, ordinary SIP or SIPS is used, media is set up by the usual SIP mechanisms, and media never traverses the overlay.
sections.eli5: Instead of a phone company keeping the phone book, all the people in the group share the job. They only help you find your friend; the actual chat happens directly between the two of you.

sections.title: Registering an AOR in the Overlay
sections.content:
A peer registers by storing a SipRegistration record under its own AOR, using the SIP-REGISTRATION Kind. The registration lifetime known from the SIP REGISTER method comes from the lifetime attribute of the basic RELOAD StoredData structure. For this document an AOR does not include the scheme (no sip:), because it has to match the rfc822Name in the X.509 certificate.

There are two kinds of mapping. A sip_registration_uri (type 1) holds another AOR, meaning "to contact me, dereference this AOR", which allows call forwarding. A sip_registration_route (type 2) holds contact preferences and a destination list, meaning "to contact me, form a connection with this Peer". A single Node-ID is just a trivial destination list.

Contact preferences use the SIP caller preferences encoding of RFC 3840. A callee can state a preferred scheme with (sip.schemes=SIP) or (sip.schemes=SIPS).

Multiple registrations for one AOR are explicitly supported. They are stored in a dictionary keyed by Node-ID, so Alice's desk phone and cell phone can each have an entry. One Node-ID may also forward to another, for example by storing key 1234 with value 5678.
sections.eli5: Each of your phones writes a small card saying where to find it. You can also write a card that says "call my friend instead", which works like call forwarding.

sections.title: Access Control and Domain Restrictions
sections.content:
To prevent hijacking, registrations follow the RELOAD USER-NODE-MATCH access control policy, and a Store is allowed only for AORs in the namespaces the overlay supports. Before a Store is permitted, the storing peer MUST check three things: the AOR is a valid Resource Name for the configured namespaces, the certificate contains a username that is a SIP AOR hashing to the Resource-ID, and the certificate contains a Node-ID equal to the dictionary key. If any check fails, the request MUST be rejected with Error_Forbidden.

These rules let Alice forward calls to Bob without his permission, but not forward Bob's calls to herself.

An overlay may restrict which domains it accepts through a <domain-restrictions> element in the overlay configuration document. If the element is absent, any AOR is accepted. If it is present with enable unset or false, only AORs matching the overlay's own domain name are accepted. If enable is true, only AORs matching one of the <pattern> elements are accepted. Each pattern is a POSIX Extended Regular Expression. The RFC gives dht\.example\.com and .*\.my\.example as examples.
sections.eli5: Only the owner of an ID card may write on their own card in the shared board, and the club can decide which kinds of names are allowed on it at all.

sections.title: Looking Up an AOR
sections.content:
A caller first decides where to look. If the AOR is a GRUU for this overlay, the callee can be contacted directly. If the domain matches a pattern configured in the overlay, the caller resolves it there and may also query DNS service records for more support of that domain. If the domain is not supported, the caller might query DNS or other discovery services for another overlay, or use standard SIP procedures. If all attempts fail, the call fails.

Resolving within the overlay takes three steps. First, Fetch the SIP-REGISTRATION Kind at the Resource-ID for the AOR, without naming dictionary keys so that all stored values come back. Second, for any result that is a non-GRUU AOR, repeat the first step for that AOR. Third, once only GRUUs and destination lists remain, remove duplicates and start SIP or SIPS connections to those peers, handling any external AORs by the proper procedure.
sections.eli5: To find a friend you look up their name on the board. If their card says "ask Sam", you look up Sam. You keep going until you get an address you can actually visit.

sections.title: Forming and Keeping a Direct Connection
sections.content:
With a set of destination lists in hand, the caller routes AppAttach messages through the overlay to each peer. The application field MUST be 5060 for SIP or 5061 for SIPS. With certificate-based authentication, the responding peer MUST present a certificate whose Node-ID matches the last entry in the destination list; otherwise the connection MUST NOT be used and MUST be closed. An existing RELOAD connection must not carry SIP messages unless it is a SIP connection, but a previously established SIP connection MAY be reused for a new call.

Once AppAttach succeeds, plain or (D)TLS-encrypted SIP flows over the connection as in normal SIP. A caller may choose SIP or SIPS but SHOULD follow the callee's contact_prefs. A callee that accepts only SIPS SHOULD say so there. All overlay links are built on (D)TLS-secured transport according to RFC 6940.

Connections formed through ICE often cross stateful NATs and firewalls, so peers must send messages often enough to keep that state alive. ICE keepalives are mandatory, so nothing more is required, and a SIP peer MAY also use keep-alive techniques from RFC 5626.
sections.eli5: After finding the address, you knock on the door and the two of you open a private line. The shared board is not used for the conversation itself. Someone has to keep nudging the line so it does not close.

sections.title: GRUUs in RELOAD
sections.content:
A Globally Routable User Agent URI (GRUU, RFC 5627) routes directly to one specific user agent instance. In RELOAD, a GRUU is built by putting a base64-encoded destination list into the gr URI parameter, using the alphabet of Table 1 in RFC 4648 except that ~ replaces =. The RFC's example is alice@example.com;gr=MDEyMzQ1Njc4OTAxMjM0NTY3ODk~.

GRUUs need no data stored in the overlay. A peer that needs to reach a GRUU in the same overlay just uses the destination list inside it and connects to that peer. Anonymous GRUUs (RFC 5767) are built the same way, but need either a different Node-ID per anonymous GRUU from the enrollment server, or a destination list containing a peer that compresses the list so the Node-ID is not revealed.
sections.eli5: A GRUU is a note with the directions to one exact door written right into it, so you do not have to look anything up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Usage defines no new RELOAD protocol elements or operations, so it adds no new threats from message exchanges. The domain restriction check is lightweight pattern matching that can run before certificate validation, so it adds no extra burden beyond the base protocol.

For SIP-specific issues, fork bombs are a much lower concern than with conventional SIP proxies, because the caller takes part in every retargeting and can count forks and throttle. Malicious retargeting, where the owner of a popular AOR points all calls at a victim, is common to SIP and hard to prevent without requiring the target to authorize every store. The RFC judges that overhead excessive.

A liberal overlay that accepts unrelated domains without authorization could allow name hijacking and bogus registrations. Mitigations are restricting namespaces, extra verification by the enrollment service, and having the caller also query DNS or other discovery services, including RFC 3263 name resolution. All SIP registration data is visible to every node in the overlay. Anonymous GRUUs can give location privacy.
sections.eli5: Because the board is public, anyone could try to write a fake card for someone else. The rules about who may write where, and double checking elsewhere, help stop that. Everything on the board can be read by everyone.
